title: The honey Dadhyanch risked his head for
hook: a sage with a horse's head teaches the honey: everything feeds everything
carry: madhu: all feeds all, one self in each
tomorrow: what do a teacher and a student say before a hard lesson?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayam atma brahma through Om: three sounds, and a silence two schools hear in their own ways. Today the Brihadaranyaka reaches the same saying through something you can taste.

Some secrets cost a head. In an old Vedic story, the sage Dadhyanch knows a secret teaching, and the god Indra warns him: teach it to anyone and your head comes off. The twin healer gods, the Ashvins, want it anyway. So they give Dadhyanch a horse's head, and he teaches them through it. Indra strikes it off, and the Ashvins put the sage's own head back on. The secret was called the honey. The Brihadaranyaka tells us what it said.
screen: `TEACH IT AND LOSE YOUR HEAD.` → `A HORSE'S HEAD, A SECRET TOLD.` → `THEY CALLED IT THE HONEY.`

segments.voice: The passage is called the honey teaching, madhu. It goes around the world one thing at a time. This earth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this earth. The waters, the same. Fire, wind, the sun, the sky, the moon, lightning, thunder: each one honey for all beings, and all beings honey for it. Nothing here only gives or only takes. Everything feeds, and is fed. And in each one, the text says, there is a shining, deathless person, and the same shining person within the body. That one is the self. Then the close: this self is Brahman, the experiencer of all. That's the honey Dadhyanch risked his head for, and it's a core Hindu teaching: the world isn't a pile of separate things using each other up. It's one web, and the same self shines in every strand. And with it, a set is complete. Tradition gathers four great sayings, one from the Upanishads of each Veda: prajnanam brahma, from the Aitareya; aham brahmasmi, from the Brihadaranyaka; tat tvam asi, from the Chandogya; and ayam atma brahma, from the Mandukya. Each Vedanta school reads them in its own way, and now all four have had their turn.
screen: `MADHU: THE HONEY TEACHING.` · `EVERYTHING FEEDS, AND IS FED.` · `THE SAME SHINING PERSON WITHIN.` · then, large: `FOUR SAYINGS, ONE FROM EACH VEDA.`

segments.voice: If there's honey near you, or anything sweet, take a little and let it rest on your tongue before you swallow. Trace it back: the flower, the rain, the ground, the hands that carried it to you. If there's nothing to taste, breathe in slowly and notice the air feeding you, and your breath warming it in return.
Ayam atma brahma, the honey way: everything feeds and is fed, and in each, the same shining self. The last day with this saying.
For the road: everything feeds and is fed, and the same self shines in each. That was the honey Dadhyanch risked his head for. Four sayings, done.

howItsDone: Students of the Brihadaranyaka read the honey teaching (2.5) as one long passage, and teachers often present the four mahavakyas together, one from the Upanishads of each Veda, at the end of studying them.
